sources.title: Popol Vuh
sources.author: K'iche' Maya priests
sources.excerpt: This is the account of how all was in suspense, all calm, in silence; all motionless, still, and the expanse of the sky was empty. This is the first account, the first narrative.
sources.longExcerpt: This is the account of how all was in suspense, all calm, in silence; all motionless, still, and the expanse of the sky was empty. This is the first account, the first narrative. This sacred book of the K'iche' Maya, written down in 1550 but preserving much older oral traditions, tells of the creation of the world and the origins of Maya civilization.

sources.title: Cahokia Mounds: The Great American City
sources.author: Mississippian culture (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: Cahokia, located near modern St. Louis, was the largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, with a population estimated at 10,000-20,000 at its peak around 1100-1200 CE. The city featured over 120 earthen mounds, the largest being Monks Mound - a massive four-terraced platform mound 30 meters tall covering 6 hectares, larger at its base than the Great Pyramid of Giza. The city was planned around a central plaza with a wooden palisade wall, residential neighborhoods organized by social class, and a sophisticated wooden calendar circle ('Woodhenge') for tracking solstices and equinoxes. Archaeological evidence reveals copper workshops, shell bead production, long-distance trade in marine shells from the Gulf Coast and obsidian from the Rockies, elite burials with elaborate grave goods, and evidence of human sacrifice.
sources.longExcerpt: Cahokia, located in the Mississippi River floodplain near modern St. Louis, Illinois, was the largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, with a population estimated at 10,000-20,000 people at its peak around 1100-1200 CE - larger than London at the same time. The city was the political, religious, and economic center of the Mississippian culture, which flourished from approximately 800-1600 CE across the Eastern Woodlands. Cahokia featured over 120 earthen mounds constructed by carrying basketloads of soil - no beasts of burden were available in pre-Columbian North America. The largest, Monks Mound, is a massive four-terraced platform mound rising 30 meters high and covering 6 hectares at its base, making it larger at the base than the Great Pyramid of Giza. A massive wooden building once stood atop the summit, likely the residence of the paramount chief and the center of religious ceremonies. The city was carefully planned around a central Grand Plaza covering 20 hectares, with residential neighborhoods organized by social class radiating outward. A wooden palisade wall 3 kilometers long with watchtowers enclosed the central precinct, built and rebuilt four times, suggesting either defensive needs or boundary maintenance between sacred and profane space. Archaeological excavations revealed sophisticated wooden calendar circles called 'Woodhenges' - circles of massive red cedar posts used to track solstices, equinoxes, and other astronomical events for agricultural and ceremonial purposes. Material culture includes copper workshops producing ritual objects, shell bead production centers, pottery showing distinctive Ramey Incised and Powell Plain styles, stone tools, and evidence of long-distance trade in marine shells from the Gulf Coast, mica from the Appalachians, and obsidian from the Rocky Mountains. Elite burials, particularly in Mound 72, contained elaborate grave goods: a 'beaded burial' where a male was laid on a platform of 20,000 marine shell beads arranged in the shape of a falcon, surrounded by bundles of arrows, mica sheets, and chunkey stones (gaming stones for a ritual sport). The same mound contained mass burials of over 50 young women aged 15-25, likely sacrificial victims, and several decapitated and handless male burials. Cahokia's rapid rise around 1050 CE (possibly triggered by a Supernova observed in 1054 CE interpreted as a divine sign) and equally rapid decline around 1350 CE (possibly due to environmental degradation, climate change, political instability, or disease) remain subjects of intense archaeological research.

citation.modernSource: Extensive excavations by archaeologists since 1960s, major studies by Timothy Pauketat and others

sources.title: Chaco Canyon Great Houses
sources.author: Ancestral Puebloan culture (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: Chaco Canyon in northwestern New Mexico was the ceremonial and political center of the Ancestral Puebloan world from approximately 850-1150 CE. The canyon contains 15 major complexes called 'great houses' - massive multi-story stone buildings constructed with precisely cut sandstone blocks. Pueblo Bonito, the largest, contained over 600 rooms and 40 kivas (ceremonial chambers), rising four stories high with walls perfectly aligned to cardinal directions. The great houses were connected by a network of prehistoric roads radiating outward up to 150 kilometers, engineered with remarkable precision - dead straight, 9 meters wide, with stairways carved into cliff faces. The buildings show sophisticated astronomical alignments marking solstices and lunar standstills.
sources.longExcerpt: Chaco Canyon in the San Juan Basin of northwestern New Mexico was the ceremonial, political, and economic center of the Ancestral Puebloan (Anasazi) world from approximately 850-1150 CE, controlling a regional system extending across 100,000 square kilometers. The canyon, though remote and arid with limited agricultural potential, contains 15 major architectural complexes called 'great houses' - massive multi-story stone buildings unlike anything built before or after in the Southwest. Pueblo Bonito, the largest and most famous, contained over 600 rooms and 40 kivas (circular underground ceremonial chambers), rising four stories high and covering nearly 2 acres. The construction required cutting and hauling over 200,000 wooden beams from forests 75 kilometers away (tree-ring dating shows specific cutting dates in the 1000s CE), and shaping an estimated 30,000 tons of sandstone blocks using stone tools. The walls were built using distinctive Chacoan masonry styles with precisely cut veneer stones facing rubble cores, creating geometric patterns. The great houses were perfectly aligned to cardinal directions and showed sophisticated astronomical alignments: windows, doors, and wall niches marked summer and winter solstices, equinoxes, and the 18.6-year lunar standstill cycle. The buildings were connected to over 75 outlier communities by a network of prehistoric roads radiating outward up to 150 kilometers, engineered with remarkable precision - dead straight regardless of terrain, 9 meters wide, with stairways carved into cliff faces and ramps over mesas. The purpose of these roads remains debated - they appear over-engineered for simple trade, suggesting ritual or ceremonial significance, possibly pilgrimage routes. Archaeological evidence shows Chaco imported massive quantities of luxury goods: turquoise from mines in the Cerrillos hills, macaw feathers and copper bells from Mesoamerica (1,500 km south), shells from the Gulf of California and Pacific Ocean, and pottery from dozens of regional production centers. The great houses contained surprisingly few domestic artifacts (hearths, grinding stones, food remains), suggesting they served primarily as ceremonial centers and elite residences rather than normal villages. Around 1130-1150 CE, a severe drought combined with possible political upheaval led to Chaco's abandonment. Descendants of the Chacoan people include modern Pueblo peoples including Hopi, Zuni, and Rio Grande Pueblos, who maintain oral traditions about Chaco and conduct pilgrimages to the canyon.

citation.modernSource: Archaeological research beginning in 1890s, extensive excavations by University of New Mexico and National Park Service

sources.title: Mesa Verde Cliff Dwellings
sources.author: Ancestral Puebloan culture (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: Mesa Verde in southwestern Colorado contains over 600 cliff dwellings built into alcoves in canyon walls, constructed between approximately 1190-1280 CE. Cliff Palace, the largest, contains 150 rooms and 23 kivas built from sandstone blocks, adobe mortar, and wooden beams, housing an estimated 100 people. The cliff dwellings required hauling all building materials and water up steep trails. These spectacular structures were occupied for less than 100 years before being abandoned around 1285 CE, possibly due to a 23-year drought, resource depletion, or social conflict. The buildings show advanced masonry techniques, with precisely fitted stones, plastered walls decorated with geometric designs, and multi-story construction wedged into natural alcoves.
sources.longExcerpt: Mesa Verde ('Green Table' in Spanish) in southwestern Colorado contains over 5,000 archaeological sites including more than 600 cliff dwellings built into natural alcoves in the sandstone canyon walls, constructed by Ancestral Puebloan people between approximately 1190-1280 CE. The cliff dwellings represent the final phase of 700+ years of occupation in the Mesa Verde region - earlier residents built pithouses and pueblos on the mesa tops before moving into the protected cliff alcoves in the late 1100s. Cliff Palace, the largest cliff dwelling in North America, contains 150 rooms and 23 kivas (ceremonial chambers) built from shaped sandstone blocks mortared with adobe (mud and straw mixture) and supported by wooden beams (vigas), housing an estimated 100 people. The multi-story structures were wedged into a natural alcove 27 meters deep, 18 meters high, and 90 meters long, with walls plastered and decorated with geometric designs in red, white, and black pigments. Building in the cliffs required tremendous effort - all construction materials (stones, wooden beams, water for mortar), household goods, food, and water for daily use had to be hauled up steep trails using tumplines (carrying straps across the forehead) and handholds chipped into the cliff face. The alcoves provided natural protection from summer heat and winter cold, and may have offered defensive advantages or spiritual significance. Archaeological evidence shows the inhabitants grew corn, beans, and squash on the mesa tops using dry farming techniques, hunted mule deer and rabbits, gathered pinyon nuts and yucca, and created distinctive black-on-white pottery, woven baskets, feather blankets, and cotton textiles. These spectacular structures were occupied for less than 100 years before being completely abandoned around 1285 CE. The reasons for abandonment are debated but likely included a severe 23-year drought documented in tree rings (1276-1299 CE), depletion of local resources (game, timber, arable land), soil erosion and arroyo-cutting making farming difficult, and possibly increasing social conflict and violence documented by skeletal trauma and burned structures. The inhabitants migrated south and east to the Rio Grande valley and Hopi mesas, where their descendants built new pueblos and maintain oral traditions about Mesa Verde as an ancestral home. The dwellings were rediscovered by ranchers in the 1880s and became one of America's first national parks in 1906.

citation.modernSource: Discovered 1888, extensive archaeological research by National Park Service and universities

sources.title: Poverty Point Earthworks
sources.author: Archaic period Native Americans (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: Poverty Point in northeastern Louisiana, dating to 1700-1100 BCE, represents one of the earliest and most complex earthwork sites in North America, predating agriculture in the region. The site features six concentric C-shaped earthen ridges, each 1-2 meters high and 25 meters wide, forming a vast amphitheater 1.2 kilometers across. The ridges contained house sites for an estimated 1,000-3,000 people. A massive earthen mound shaped like a bird with outstretched wings rises 21 meters high - the largest earthwork construction in the Americas at that time. The society was pre-agricultural hunter-gatherers who nevertheless organized massive communal labor projects, engaged in extensive long-distance trade, and created sophisticated baked clay objects.
sources.longExcerpt: Poverty Point in northeastern Louisiana, dating to approximately 1700-1100 BCE (Late Archaic period), represents one of the earliest and most complex earthwork sites in North America and challenges assumptions about what pre-agricultural societies could achieve. The site features six concentric C-shaped earthen ridges arranged in a vast amphitheater pattern opening toward the Mississippi River floodplain. Each ridge stands 1-2 meters high, measures 25 meters wide, and the entire configuration spans 1.2 kilometers across, covering 200 hectares. Post molds discovered on the ridge tops show the ridges were residential areas containing hundreds of houses built from wooden posts with thatched roofs, housing an estimated population of 1,000-3,000 people. The largest mound, Mound A, shaped like a bird in flight with outstretched wings when viewed from above, rises 21 meters high and measures 200 x 220 meters at the base - the largest earthwork construction in the Americas at that time, requiring an estimated 238,500 cubic meters of soil carried in baskets. The society was pre-agricultural, subsisting on hunting (deer, bear, turkey, waterfowl), fishing, and gathering (acorns, hickory nuts, wild plants from the rich bottomlands), yet organized the massive communal labor needed to construct these earthworks. Poverty Point was a major trade and ceremonial center with artifacts from across eastern North America: copper from the Great Lakes, hematite and galena from Missouri, slate from the Appalachians, jasper from Pennsylvania, quartz crystal from Arkansas, and steatite from Alabama and Georgia. The people created distinctive 'Poverty Point objects' - small baked clay balls in various shapes (spheres, cylinders, cones) numbering in the hundreds of thousands, used for cooking by heating in fires and dropping into containers of food to boil water or roast meat. They also created finely carved stone beads, pendants, and bird effigies, and made stone tools using microflint technology. The site was seasonally occupied, with large gatherings for ceremonies, feasting, and trade during certain times of year, similar to later ceremonial centers. Around 1100 BCE the site was abandoned, possibly due to flooding, climate change, or social reorganization. Poverty Point demonstrates that complex societies with monumental architecture, long-distance trade, and social stratification could develop among hunter-gatherers under favorable environmental conditions, without agriculture.

citation.modernSource: Discovered 1950s, extensive excavations by archaeologists, UNESCO World Heritage Site

sources.title: Great Serpent Mound
sources.author: Fort Ancient or Adena culture (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: The Great Serpent Mound in southern Ohio is the world's largest surviving effigy mound, depicting a serpent over 400 meters long, 6 meters wide, and 1 meter high, winding along a bluff overlooking a creek. The serpent's tail is coiled in a tight spiral, its body undulates in seven deep curves, and its head is aligned with the summer solstice sunset, with jaws opening around an oval earthwork interpreted as either an egg or an eye. Dating has been controversial - radiocarbon dates suggest construction around 1070 CE by Fort Ancient culture, though the site location atop an Adena burial complex (dating to 300 BCE) suggests possible earlier construction or ritual reuse of sacred landscape.
sources.longExcerpt: The Great Serpent Mound in Adams County, southern Ohio, is the world's largest surviving effigy mound - an earthwork shaped to represent an animal or symbol. The serpent extends over 400 meters long, averages 6 meters wide and 1 meter high, and depicts a snake winding gracefully along a bluff overlooking Brush Creek. The serpent's tail is coiled in a tight triple spiral, its body undulates in seven deep curves that may align with solstice or lunar events, and its head is aligned with the summer solstice sunset, with jaws opening around an oval earthwork variously interpreted as an egg being swallowed, the sun, an eye, or a representation of a solar eclipse. The mound was constructed by piling clay, soil, and stones into the carefully planned shape, then covering it with grass. Unlike burial mounds, effigy mounds were not used for burials but served ceremonial, cosmological, or territorial marking purposes. The dating and cultural attribution of Serpent Mound has been controversial. Early archaeologists assumed it was built by the Adena culture around 300 BCE because it sits atop a low Adena burial mound complex containing stone tools and artifacts. However, radiocarbon dating of charcoal from within the serpent's body suggests construction around 1070 CE, attributing it to the later Fort Ancient culture (1000-1650 CE). Some scholars suggest the Fort Ancient people may have rebuilt or enhanced an earlier Adena construction, reusing a sacred landscape. The astronomical alignments suggest the builders possessed sophisticated knowledge of celestial events and encoded this in landscape architecture. The serpent may represent a powerful spiritual being from Native American cosmology - serpents appear in many indigenous traditions as creators, destroyers, water spirits, and symbols of renewal. The mound was nearly destroyed by farming in the 1800s before being purchased and preserved by Frederic Ward Putnam of Harvard's Peabody Museum in 1886. Recent LiDAR surveys have revealed additional earthworks and features around the serpent previously invisible to ground observers.

citation.modernSource: Preserved by Harvard's Peabody Museum (1886), ongoing archaeological research

sources.title: Olmec Colossal Heads
sources.author: Olmec civilization (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: The Olmec civilization of Mexico's Gulf Coast (1500-400 BCE) created 17 known colossal stone heads, each carved from a single basalt boulder, depicting rulers wearing distinctive helmets. The heads range from 1.5 to 3.4 meters tall and weigh 6-50 tons. Each head has unique facial features, suggesting they are portraits of specific individuals - likely powerful kings or ball game champions. The basalt was quarried from the Tuxtla Mountains and transported up to 80 kilometers through swamps and rivers to Olmec centers at San Lorenzo and La Venta, requiring enormous organizational capacity. The Olmec are considered Mesoamerica's 'mother culture,' establishing artistic, religious, and political patterns followed by later Maya and Aztec civilizations.
sources.longExcerpt: The Olmec civilization of Mexico's Gulf Coast lowlands (approximately 1500-400 BCE) is considered Mesoamerica's first major civilization and 'mother culture,' establishing artistic, religious, architectural, and political patterns that influenced all later civilizations including the Maya, Zapotec, and Aztec. The Olmec created 17 known colossal stone heads, each carved from a single basalt boulder using only stone tools (no metal tools existed in Mesoamerica at this time), depicting what appear to be rulers or elite ball game players wearing distinctive helmets with ear spools and sometimes chinstraps. The heads range from 1.5 to 3.4 meters in height and weigh between 6 and 50 tons, with the largest (San Lorenzo Head 1) weighing approximately 50 tons. Each head displays unique facial features - different nose shapes, lip sizes, eye forms - strongly suggesting they are portraits of specific historical individuals rather than generic representations, likely powerful kings (ajawtaak) who ruled Olmec city-states. The creation of these monuments required extraordinary organizational capacity. The basalt was quarried from Cerro Cintepec in the Tuxtla Mountains, then transported 60-80 kilometers through difficult terrain including swamps, rivers, and rainforest to Olmec centers at San Lorenzo, La Venta, and Tres Zapotes. The transport likely used wooden rafts, rollers, and hundreds or thousands of workers pulling with ropes, demonstrating centralized political power capable of mobilizing massive labor forces. After transporting the boulders, sculptors carved the distinctive features using stone hammers and chisels, a process requiring months or years. The heads were originally brightly painted and may have had wooden additions. Some heads show evidence of deliberate mutilation - eyes, noses, or mouths chiseled away - possibly representing ritual 'killing' of the monument after a ruler's death or defeat, or political violence between rival dynasties. The Olmec civilization also created massive earthen pyramids, sophisticated jade carvings, developed the earliest writing in the Americas (still undeciphered), invented the Mesoamerican ballgame (which became central to later Maya and Aztec culture), and established the 260-day sacred calendar and Long Count dating system used by subsequent civilizations. Olmec religious iconography featuring the were-jaguar (human-jaguar hybrid), feathered serpent, and maize god appears throughout later Mesoamerican religions.

citation.modernSource: Discovered beginning in 1862, extensive research by Matthew Stirling, Michael Coe, and others

sources.title: Teotihuacan: City of the Gods
sources.author: Teotihuacan civilization (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: Teotihuacan in central Mexico was one of the largest cities in the ancient world, with a population estimated at 125,000-200,000 at its peak around 450 CE. The city was meticulously planned along a 4-kilometer-long central avenue (the Avenue of the Dead) aligned 15.5° east of true north, possibly to track the setting of the Pleiades. The Pyramid of the Sun, third-largest pyramid in the world, rises 65 meters tall with a base covering 220 x 230 meters, containing 1 million cubic meters of material. The Pyramid of the Moon anchors the northern end of the avenue. The city featured hundreds of apartment compounds housing thousands of families, elaborate murals depicting gods and rituals, and evidence of multi-ethnic neighborhoods with immigrants from across Mesoamerica.
sources.longExcerpt: Teotihuacan ('Place Where the Gods Were Created' in Nahuatl) in central Mexico, 40 kilometers northeast of modern Mexico City, was one of the largest cities in the ancient world, with a population estimated at 125,000-200,000 people at its peak around 450 CE - larger than contemporary Rome. The city flourished from approximately 100 BCE to 550 CE and served as the political, economic, religious, and cultural center of Mesoamerica, controlling an empire or trade network extending across much of Mexico and into Guatemala. The city was meticulously planned along geometric principles with a central north-south axis called the Avenue of the Dead (Miccaotli), a 4-kilometer-long ceremonial boulevard 40 meters wide, aligned 15.5° east of true north - possibly to track the setting of the Pleiades star cluster on the date the Avenue crosses the zenith, or to align with Cerro Gordo mountain. The Pyramid of the Sun (Pirámide del Sol), the third-largest pyramid in the world after Cholula and Khufu's Great Pyramid, rises 65 meters tall with a base measuring 220 x 230 meters, containing approximately 1 million cubic meters of material carried in baskets by thousands of workers. The pyramid was built in a single construction phase around 200 CE, possibly over the top of a sacred cave (discovered in 1971) that may have been considered the place of creation. The Pyramid of the Moon (Pirámide de la Luna), though smaller, sits on higher ground and anchors the northern end of the Avenue. Excavations beneath the Pyramid of the Moon revealed multiple burials of sacrificial victims including decapitated and bound individuals, jaguars, pumas, eagles, and rattlesnakes buried alive in cages - offerings to the storm god. The city featured hundreds of multi-family residential compounds arranged in a grid pattern, each compound housing 60-100 people in interconnected rooms around central courtyards. Walls were covered with elaborate murals depicting gods (including the feathered serpent Quetzalcoatl, rain god Tlaloc, and a mysterious 'Great Goddess'), rituals, priests, warriors, and mythological scenes painted in vivid reds, blues, greens, and yellows. Archaeological evidence shows multi-ethnic neighborhoods with distinct pottery styles indicating immigrants from Oaxaca, Veracruz, and Maya regions living in separate quarters, suggesting Teotihuacan was a cosmopolitan metropolis. The city's economy was based on obsidian tool production (workshops processed volcanic glass from nearby quarries into blades traded across Mesoamerica), ceramic production, and agriculture using irrigation from the San Juan River. Around 550 CE, the city's center was deliberately burned and the elite compounds destroyed, though debate continues whether this was internal revolution, external conquest, or ritual termination. The city influenced later civilizations enormously - the Aztecs, arriving centuries after Teotihuacan's collapse, regarded it as the legendary birthplace of the current era of the world.

citation.modernSource: Extensive excavations since 1906, major research by INAH (Mexican Institute of Anthropology)

sources.title: Maya Hieroglyphic Inscriptions
sources.author: Classic Maya civilization (archaeological evidence)
sources.excerpt: The Maya developed Mesoamerica's most sophisticated writing system, with over 800 glyphs representing syllables and logograms. The longest Maya text ever discovered is the Hieroglyphic Stairway at Copan, Honduras, containing 2,200 glyphs carved on 63 stone steps recounting the dynastic history of Copan's rulers from the city's founding in 426 CE through the 8th century. Maya inscriptions carved on stone stelae, temple walls, ceramic vessels, and bark-paper codices recorded historical events, astronomical observations, mathematical calculations, and religious prophecies using a sophisticated calendar system more accurate than the European calendar of the same period.
sources.longExcerpt: The Maya developed Mesoamerica's most sophisticated writing system, a complex script combining logograms (signs representing whole words) and syllabic signs (representing sounds), with over 800 distinct glyphs capable of expressing the full range of spoken Maya languages. The longest Maya text ever discovered is the Hieroglyphic Stairway at Copan, Honduras, containing approximately 2,200 glyphs carved on 63 stone steps rising to Temple 26. The text, erected around 755 CE by K'ak' Yipyaj Chan K'awiil (Smoke Shell), the 15th ruler of Copan, recounts the dynastic history of Copan's rulers from the city's founding in 426 CE through events of the 8th century, glorifying the military victories and ritual achievements of past kings. The stairway unfortunately collapsed in antiquity, scrambling many blocks, making portions of the text difficult to reconstruct. Maya inscriptions were carved on stone monuments (stelae and altars), temple stairways, lintels and wall panels, ceramic vessels, jade and shell ornaments, and painted in bark-paper codices (folding books). They recorded historical events including royal births, accessions, marriages, military victories, and deaths; astronomical observations tracking Venus cycles, lunar eclipses, and solstices; mathematical calculations using a sophisticated base-20 positional notation system including the concept of zero (developed independently of Old World mathematicians); and religious prophecies and ritual calendar dates using both the 260-day sacred calendar (tzolk'in) and 365-day solar calendar (haab), combined in the 52-year Calendar Round. The Maya also used a Long Count system tracking days from a mythological creation date (August 11, 3114 BCE in the Gregorian calendar), allowing them to record dates over thousands of years. Maya astronomy was remarkably accurate - their calculation of the solar year (365.2420 days) was more precise than the Julian calendar used in Europe at the same time (which calculated 365.25 days; the actual value is 365.2422 days). The inscriptions reveal Maya civilization was not peaceful and theocratic as once believed, but comprised warring city-states led by powerful kings (k'uhul ajaw, 'divine lords') who waged constant warfare for tribute, sacrificial captives, and political dominance. Famous inscriptions include Palenque's Temple of Inscriptions (containing King Pakal's tomb with a sarcophagus lid showing the king falling into the underworld), Tikal's carved wooden lintels, Bonampak's painted murals showing brutal warfare and captive torture, and the four surviving Maya codices (Dresden, Madrid, Paris, and Grolier). The decipherment of Maya writing, achieved primarily in the 1960s-1990s through the work of Yuri Knorosov, Linda Schele, David Stuart, and others, revolutionized understanding of Maya civilization.

citation.originalPublication: Mesoamerica, c. 300 BCE - 1500 CE (Classic period 250-900 CE)
citation.modernSource: Decipherment by Yuri Knorosov, Tatiana Proskouriakoff, Linda Schele, David Stuart, and others
